title: Message in a coral

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Palmyra and surrounding islands in the tropical Pacific Ocean are of interest to climatologists because they lie at the centre of Earth's most powerful climate force, the sea current El Niño. This huge flow of water, which recurs every three to seven years, transfers huge amounts of heat across the equatorial Pacific Ocean. Palmyra's corals have revealed that, out of five selected time periods between AD 928 and 1998, the largest short-term climate variability occurred between 1635 and 1670 - rather than during the twentieth century, despite the presence of global warming.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Kim Cobb, now at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena, and her colleagues drilled into rare deposits of fossilised coral that were probably torn off their reefs and swept onto the island during large storms over the past millennium. The fossils reveal the water temperature and levels of salt at the time when the corals were growing. From corals deposited at different periods along Palmyra’s beaches, the team reconstructed the variability of past climate in the region on a month-to-month basis. 'What Kim Cobb has done at Palmyra is unique,' says climatologist Rob Dunbar of Stanford University in California.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Cobb's research suggests that the powerful El Niño cycles which we have experienced in recent decades are well within the natural range. What's more, the corals hint that El Niño is independent of the mean climate, at least within the range of recorded temperatures. So the cycle may not be as sensitive to global warming as has been feared.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The equatorial Pacific has often been compared to a giant bathtub - a layer of warm water sits on top of colder bottom waters. Easterly trade winds constantly sweep its sun-heated surface towards Indonesia, exposing cold water at the Chilean and Peruvian coasts. As we know, when El Niño begins its cycle, these trade winds diminish, allowing warm water to gather off Chile and Peru. The resulting heat flow has profound effects on climate and ecology on both sides of the ocean. The pendulum's return swing is called La Niña. This brings cool water to the South American coast, while a new warm pool gathers off South-east Asia, ready for the next cycle.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The worldwide consequences of this variation can be dramatic - perhaps unsurprisingly, given that the Pacific Ocean spans two-fifths of the Equator and stores an enormous amount of heat. The 1997/98 El Niño, for example, caused severe droughts that set vast tracts of Indonesian timber on fire. South America, meanwhile, suffered storms and flooding. During a typical warm phase, fish such as the Pacific skipjack tuna move east and maize yields in Argentina go up; rainfall in southern Africa declines dramatically, and the northern United States enjoys warm, dry winters.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Pacific climate variability is nothing new. Scientists engaged in botanical research have noted similar rhythms when examining the annual growth rings in semi-fossilised tree trunks buried in Chile about 50,000 years ago. But the strong and long El Niño events of the late twentieth century have led some experts to speculate that global warming is forcing the effects of this powerful force to new heights. A lot of money is at stake. David Changnon, a geographer at the Northern Illinois University in DeKalb, estimates that the 1997/98 El Niño ultimately boosted the US economy by as much as US$18 billion. The northern states' warm, dry winter led to gains in terms of lower costs for transport, construction and retail businesses and domestic heating bills too. The south of the country, however, lost between US$4 billion and US$6 billion in flood damage. Elsewhere in the world, the balance may be different, but the numbers will still be large.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Computer models - our only chance of testing out the effects of climate change - have not been very enlightening on the subject of El Niño's future. Different models respond so differently to global warming that they yield evidence to suit every political agenda. Hence, the excitement about Cobb's research results. They show El Niño playing to its own tune, apparently without much connection to mean global climate or greenhouse-gas emissions - so far. No wonder computer models are divided. But this independence will not save us from torrential rains or blazing droughts caused by climate change - there is now a scientific consensus that the effects of modern life and technology are probably making extreme weather events worse.

subtitle: New research has been done into El Niño, the Pacific Ocean current which recurs every few years and which has a huge impact on climate in the region. Heike Langenberg reports
